$comment: FrontierJS — related projects register. tier = thesis proximity (1 nearest). closeness = literal code/API-shape similarity to FJS, 0-100. inspiration = how much Kobami actually learned from it, 0-100 (guessed, edit manually). stance + fjsWay = what FJS actually DID with what it took — the reflection, not the source. Keep fjsWay honest: 'not yet' is a legitimate answer and appears here several times.

tier.1: Direct lineage — same thesis, study hardest

scales.closeness: 0-100. How literally similar the code, API shapes, and vocabulary are to FJS.
scales.inspiration: 0-100. How much was actually taken from it. Manually maintained.
scales.$stanceFormat: Each value is 'short label — explanation'. The site chips the part before the dash and uses the rest as its tooltip, so keep the label to two or three words.

stance.adopted: Taken as it is — same shape, same vocabulary, little changed
stance.extended: Taken further — pushed past where the source stopped
stance.spirit: The idea, not the mechanism — the concept taken, the mechanics refused
stance.declined: Looked at and left — considered closely, deliberately not taken
stance.warning: Studied as a failure — the design is shaped by avoiding it
stance.pending: A debt not yet paid — named, not yet acted on

projects.name: Feathers.js
projects.relation: Direct ancestor of Junction. find/get/create/patch/remove, before/after/around/error hooks, channels + publish, $limit/$skip.
projects.gap: Never closed the Data gap — service is not derived from schema.
projects.fjsWay: Copied almost verbatim, down to the method names and the four hook phases, because they were already right. What Junction added is the half Feathers leaves to you: the service is read out of the Model, so CRUD, the 400s and the 401s arrive without a service file. Feathers' generator writes you a publisher; here the service declares `channel:` and the announcement happens once, in the call, where no handler can forget it.

projects.name: Wasp
projects.relation: Spec-driven, batteries-included, explicit whole-app declaration. Nearest thesis twin.
projects.gap: Dropped its custom DSL for a TypeScript spec in June 2026 after 5 years. Read the post-mortem before touching .lite.
projects.fjsWay: The whole-app declaration is the shared thesis and was taken gladly. The retreat from a custom DSL was not — knowingly, and with the post-mortem read. The bet is that a DSL only earns its cost if it is the seed of more than one realm: .lite feeds the migration, the API's validation and the browser's field rules from one file. If it were only feeding the ORM, Wasp would be right and this would be a TypeScript object.

projects.name: Convex
projects.relation: schema.ts to reactive queries to real-time by default. Live-by-default is core, not bolt-on.
projects.gap: Push-from-query rather than push-from-mutation-event. Costlier than FJS, correct more often.
projects.fjsWay: Took the expectation — that live is the default state of an application, not a feature you bolt on — and refused the mechanism. Convex tracks what each query read and re-runs it; FJS announces the mutation and lets the client decide. That is cheaper and simpler, and it is honestly worse: a derived view nobody announced goes stale here and cannot there. Filed as a known trade, not a win.

projects.name: ZenStack v3
projects.relation: Prisma schema plus access policies declared in the schema. Literally gates. Record-level auth reference.
projects.gap: Policy language grew a full expression grammar — schema overreach.
projects.fjsWay: The idea is taken whole — access declared on the model, compiled into the query, beneath every caller — and then pushed one realm further: the same declaration crosses the wire, so `resource.can()` answers in the browser from the rule the migration came from. Its overreach is taken as the warning: the policy language here stays deliberately small, and anything wanting a service call is a hook instead. A grammar in the schema is how a schema stops being readable.

projects.name: RedwoodJS / CedarJS
projects.relation: schema to SDL to cells to UI, Prisma-rooted. Source of the Cell pattern.
projects.gap: Redwood GraphQL wound down; CedarJS is the maintained fork. The Redwood name now means RedwoodSDK (Cloudflare/RSC), unrelated.
projects.fjsWay: The Cell — a component that declares its own loading, empty and failure states alongside its query — is the shape `createResource` is reaching for, without GraphQL underneath it or a code generator between the two. The SDL layer was the part declined: it is a second description of data that already had one, and every layer like that is a place for the two to disagree.

projects.name: Meteor
projects.relation: Original live-by-default and isomorphic stack.
projects.gap: Died of coupling. Read as autopsy — what happens when intentional gaps get closed too.
projects.fjsWay: Read as an autopsy, and it is the direct reason the realms here are named and separable rather than fused. Mesa is a true leaf with zero workspace dependencies; the API realm survives even where it could be dissolved; every package is meant to be usable alone. Meteor proved that closing every seam feels wonderful for two years and then cannot be escaped. The gaps in FJS are deliberate, and this is who taught that.

projects.name: Phoenix / Ecto / Channels
projects.relation: Source of the Channel vocabulary. Contexts map closely to realms.
projects.gap: Ecto changesets — validation as a value that travels, not a hook side-effect. Not yet adopted in FJS.
projects.fjsWay: The Channel vocabulary was taken as-is, and Contexts are the closest prior art for the realms. The changeset is the outstanding debt and the most interesting idea on this page: validation as a value you can pass around, inspect and combine, rather than a hook that throws on the way past. FJS validates in a hook today. That is not a decision — it is just what has been built so far.

projects.name: Remult
projects.relation: TS entity as single source of truth to REST plus frontend client plus admin. Same thesis, tiny surface.
projects.gap: Not yet studied. Closest thing to a control experiment for the FJS thesis.
projects.fjsWay: Nothing has been taken, and that is the entry. It reaches the same conclusion — one declaration, radiating to server and client — from a TypeScript entity rather than a schema file, on a fraction of the surface area. Either it shows the DSL is unnecessary, or it shows exactly what a DSL buys. Both answers are worth having and neither has been earned yet.

projects.name: AdonisJS
projects.relation: Closest Node analog for structure, CLI, and conventions. fli should feel like ace.
projects.gap: Schema is not the seed — models are classes.
projects.fjsWay: The ergonomics were taken and the model layer was not. fli is measured against ace, the directory conventions against Adonis's, and the general principle that a Node framework may have opinions is largely its example. But a model that is a class is a second description of the table; here the table and the class are both readings of one file.

projects.name: Supabase
projects.relation: schema to API plus realtime plus RLS, generated. RLS is the gate system in Postgres form.
projects.gap: Proof that declared access scales. No application realm above it.
projects.fjsWay: It supplies the evidence rather than the code: declared row-level access works at real scale, which is the load-bearing assumption under `@@allow`. What FJS builds on top is the part Supabase leaves to you — an application realm with services, hooks and jobs, in the same vocabulary rather than in whatever you brought. And no company in the middle: the same idea over a SQLite file you own.

projects.name: Payload CMS
projects.relation: Config-as-code collections to REST/GraphQL/admin, with hooks and per-operation access functions. Near-identical shape to Model plus Service plus Gate.
projects.gap: Access is imperative functions, not declared attributes.
projects.fjsWay: The shape arrived at independently and matches almost line for line — collection, hooks, per-operation access — which is the best evidence that the shape is right. The difference is one word: access there is a function you write, access here is an attribute you declare. A function can only run where someone calls it; an attribute compiles into the query and holds for callers written later.

projects.name: Blitz.js
projects.relation: The zero-API thesis. Mostly dead.
projects.gap: Removing the API realm entirely was the wrong cut. FJS kept it as an intentional gap — that was right.
projects.fjsWay: The lesson taken is negative and it is one of the most valuable on the page: the API realm is not ceremony to be abolished. It is where authorization, validation and the wire contract live, and an app that dissolves it has not removed the work — it has scattered it. FJS keeps the boundary and spends its effort making it cost almost nothing to declare.

projects.name: Sails.js / Waterline
projects.relation: Blueprint routes auto-generated from models, realtime blueprints over sockets. The 2014 version of this idea.
projects.gap: Lost because the ORM had no schema authority. Study the failure directly.
projects.fjsWay: This is the derived API, twelve years early, and it is worth being humble about that. It lost because the ORM was permissive: the model was a suggestion, so the routes derived from it were a suggestion too. The single non-negotiable in FJS is the answer to exactly that — the .lite file is the authority, the database is migrated to match it, and the ORM reads it rather than defining it.

projects.name: LoopBack 4
projects.relation: Model to API automatically, with ACLs declared on the model. Same gate instinct.
projects.gap: Drowned in decorators. Cautionary case for declaration ergonomics.
projects.fjsWay: Same instinct, opposite ergonomics, and the reason declarations here are attributes rather than decorators. `@@gate("0.4.4.5")` on the model is one line you can read at a glance; the equivalent in decorator form is a paragraph of imports and generics wrapped around the thing it describes. Being declarative is not enough — the declaration has to stay smaller than what it replaces.

projects.name: Encore.ts
projects.relation: Infrastructure declared in code, provisioned from the declaration. Best available model for the Manifest to Release pattern.
projects.gap: Nobody else does declaration to realization this cleanly at the infra level. Under-studied.
projects.fjsWay: It is the model for the realm FJS has built least of. Release exists as a noun and a deploy pipeline; declaration-to-provisioned-infrastructure is still aspiration. Encore has done it more cleanly than anyone and has been read too little. When the Manifest becomes something an operator acts on rather than something a page renders, it will be walking a path this project already mapped.

projects.name: Ruby on Rails
projects.relation: Convention over configuration. Kamal 2 is already the FJS deploy model.
projects.gap: Migrations, not schema-as-seed. Schema is the output, not the input.
projects.fjsWay: The disposition is inherited almost entirely: conventions over configuration, one blessed layout, a framework with opinions and a CLI that acts on them. Kamal is the deploy model more or less as-is. The one place FJS turns the other way is the important one — in Rails the schema is the output of the migrations, here the migration is the output of the schema. Everything else on this page follows from that inversion.

projects.name: Laravel
projects.relation: Forge and Vapor are the Basecamp precedent. Ecosystem-as-product.
projects.gap: Same schema-as-output problem as Rails.
projects.fjsWay: The standard for what 'complete' means: a queue, a scheduler, mail, notifications, policies and a CLI that all know about each other. app.notify is Laravel's notification design nearly unchanged, and the tooling story around Basecamp is Forge's precedent. What is taken further is reach — those batteries stop at the response here they keep going, so the browser gets the field rules and the gate rather than a client SDK and a fresh start.

projects.name: Prisma + tRPC
projects.relation: The assembled alternative FJS argues against. The honest comparison.
projects.gap: Type safety across the wire, but no runtime coherence. Types are not gates.
projects.fjsWay: .lite deliberately wears Prisma's syntax — `model`, scalar then attributes — so nobody has to learn a new shape to read it, and that debt should be stated more often than it is. What is refused is stopping at compile time. Types vanish at runtime: they cannot filter a query by owner, reject a 60-character title, or tell a button it is not allowed. The schema here is read while the program runs, which is the whole argument.

projects.name: AWS Amplify Gen 2
projects.relation: TS schema to data plus auth plus API in one declaration. Same radiation.
projects.gap: Worse ergonomics, vendor-locked. Radiation without coherence.
projects.fjsWay: Proof that the radiation is not the hard part. One declaration producing data, auth and an API is achievable and has been achieved — and it still is not pleasant to use, because the pieces it produces do not share a vocabulary or a place to stand. Coherence is the product. It is also the argument for staying self-hostable: the same derivation with a vendor underneath it is a different deal entirely.

projects.name: SvelteKit
projects.relation: Sierra's direct model. File-system routing, load(), prefetch, layouts. .mesa maps to .svelte, script module maps to Svelte's module context block.
projects.gap: No Data or API realm. Sierra inherits the shape but not the seed.
projects.fjsWay: Taken about as directly as anything here: file-tree routing, layout chains, load-then-render, the single-file component with a module block. Someone who knows SvelteKit can read Sierra without being taught it, and that is the intent rather than an accident. The one thing added is what the route binds to — a Resource that already carries the schema's field rules and its gate, instead of a fetch you write.

projects.name: SolidJS
projects.relation: Mesa's reactivity model. Fine-grained signals, compile-away components, no virtual DOM. createSignal maps directly to Mesa's runtime primitives.
projects.gap: Library, not framework. Mesa takes the runtime, Sierra supplies everything above it.
projects.fjsWay: The reactivity model is taken wholesale — fine-grained signals, components that run once, no virtual DOM, ownership scopes for anything with a lifetime. Mesa's runtime primitives are recognisably the same primitives. What sits on top is a compiler that owns the template, which is what lets one component render to a live DOM, to static HTML with islands, or to table-based markup for an email.
